transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Daniel Ortiz (CTO, SummitScale), Maya Li (Lead ML Eng), Owen Brooks (Infra)

Summary:
Technical deep dive focused on prefix/prompt caching strategy: cache keys, hit rates, multi-tenant safety, KV-cache sizing, batching interactions, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Customer wants predictable latency under 100ms p95 for chat flows and safe multi-tenant isolation for shared Dedicated pools.

Topics covered:
- Current SummitScale stack and traffic patterns
- What constitutes a cache key (prompt prefixes, conversation context, persona tokens)
- TTLs and eviction policies vs. cost/space tradeoffs
- Tenant isolation strategies (namespacing, encryption-at-rest, per-tenant caches)
- Interaction between batching and prefix cache (hit amplification vs. latency tail)
- Quantization impacts on cache compatibility and hit correctness
- On-prem/VPC networking implications for cache synchronization and cold-starts

Shared artifacts referenced:
- Prefix-caching benchmark spreadsheet (link): https://redwood.share/prefix-cache-benchmarks-2025 (internal)
- Quickstart doc for on-prem cache agent: /drive/Redwood/ops/onprem-cache-agent.md
- Example prompt templates (shared in follow-up)

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Hayes: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Um, quick roll call?
[00:07] Daniel Ortiz: Daniel here. Hi.
[00:09] Maya Li: Maya on the call. Hey.
[00:11] Owen Brooks: Owen, infra.
[00:13] Priya Nair: Priya from Redwood, SE. Jordan, you want to kick off?
[00:17] Jordan Hayes: Yeah, yeah. Thanks. So the purpose is a deep dive on prefix caching for your chat product, so we can figure hit rates, safety, and what pilot looks like. Quick ask from our side: what's your current traffic shape and avg prefix lengths?
[00:29] Maya Li: Sure, so uh, we have about 80 rps steady state across user-facing chat, bursts to around 350 during business hours, and median prefix length, uh, for prompts is about 240 tokens but long-tail goes up to, like, 900 when people paste code blocks.
[00:44] Daniel Ortiz: Important bit: we need p95 latency under 100ms for simple assistant responses, otherwise product team will push back.
[00:50] Priya Nair: Got it. That shapes how aggressive we can be with batching and caching. If you want 100ms p95, we lean more to prefix hits and smaller batch sizes to avoid queuing tail.
[01:03] Owen Brooks: Also, we have a hybrid infra — some traffic must stay in our VPC, we can't route it through hosted region because of residency. On-prem option is a plus.
[01:12] Jordan Hayes: Ok, perfect context. Let's walk through what we typically put into a cache key. Priya?
[01:17] Priya Nair: Yeah. So, cache key is the canonicalized prompt prefix, model id + weights/quantization tag, temperature/top-k meta, and tenant-id/namespace. Important to normalize whitespace, variable names, and redact PII. Also we recommend including the KV-cache shape: sequence length and attention mask hash so the runtime can validate compatibility of cached KV blobs.
[01:36] Maya Li: Wait, if we include model quantization tag, doesn't that mean re-encode when we switch quantization? We often test int8 vs int4.
[01:42] Priya Nair: Right — the cache entry must include a kernel/quantization fingerprint. If you change quantization, old cached KV may be incompatible. We either invalidate on deploy or maintain multiple namespace variants per model-quant tag. That adds space but keeps hits correct.
[01:56] Daniel Ortiz: How big does the KV blob get? Our GPU memory is limited on-prem.
[02:01] Priya Nair: Blob size roughly proportional to hidden_size * sequence_len * element_size. Eg for 16k context  and 1B-ish model maybe tens to hundreds of MB per long prefix. For typical 240-token prefixes for your stack it's, uh, modest — single-digit MBs per entry for many quantized runtimes. But long-tail 900 tokens will be larger. We recommend TTL + size-limited LRU and optional compression.
[02:23] Owen Brooks: Compression good. But we need multi-tenant safety — we can't have cross-tenant leakage if we run a shared Dedicated pool. How do you enforce that?
[02:31] Priya Nair: Two layers: logical namespacing of keys (tenant-id in the key) plus ACLs at the cache-service level. For extra safety we support per-tenant encryption keys: the KV blob is encrypted with customer-specific KMS keys before being persisted. That way even accidental cross-read is garbage.
[02:47] Maya Li: For on-prem, can we manage KMS locally?
[02:50] Jordan Hayes: Yes, Private deployments support customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll provide network diagram and integration doc.
[02:56] Daniel Ortiz: Good. Next — hit rates. What's a realistic hit rate for conversational assistants?
[03:01] Priya Nair: In our benchmarks, for session-based assistants with lots of repetition we see 50-75% prefix hit for conservative keying (tenant + canonicalized prefix + model tag). If you coarsen keys (strip non-essential tokens or collapse variable placeholders), you can raise hit rates but at risk of semantic mismatch. We should test with your prompt templates.
[03:20] Maya Li: We do have many templated prompts — system messages + user template + user input. Expect decent reuse. We'll send examples.
[03:26] Priya Nair: Great. Also note batching interacts: if you batch aggressively to improve throughput, you may add queuing time which hurts p95. But batching can increase hit-density because multiple similar requests arrive together and we can reuse KV in-memory. There's a tradeoff.
[03:41] Owen Brooks: On on-prem, how do you keep cache warm across restarts or autoscaling? We can't tolerate cold-start latency spikes.
[03:49] Priya Nair: A couple options: persistent cache on fast NVMe, warm-up hooks during rollout (preload top-N prefixes based on logs), and cross-node cache replication for hot keys. For strict isolation, replication only replicates keys within the same tenant namespace.
[04:02] Jordan Hayes: Could also use predictive prefetch: when a conversation hits certain patterns, prefetch the next likely prefixes. More complex but good for deterministic flows.
[04:11] Maya Li: Hmm. For privacy reasons we can't prefetch across different users, but within same session it's fine.
[04:16] Priya Nair: Right. Prefetch stays in-session.
[04:19] Daniel Ortiz: Any concern about consistency if we do per-node caches and lose a node?
[04:23] Priya Nair: If strict consistency needed, we use a centralized cache store; for lower latencies we use local-memo caches plus a backing store. On Dedicated we let customers pick — we can run a replicated Redis-like layer in the VPC or a local file-backed cache with fast replication.
[04:37] Owen Brooks: Can we scope cache invalidation to a tenant when we roll a new policy?
[04:40] Priya Nair: Yes, we support namespace invalidation and tag-based invalidation. You can push a 'model:quant-tag' flip and invalidate only those entries.
[04:47] Maya Li: About quantization: do cached KV blobs from an int8 run meaningfully differ versus int4? If we have the same logical outputs but different numerical format, can we reuse?
[04:56] Priya Nair: Generally no — underlying kernel math changes element layout or precision so it's unsafe to reuse cross-quant modes. We include quant-tag to avoid mismatches. In some cases with compatible runtimes we might convert on the fly but that's expensive and negates latency wins.
[05:09] Daniel Ortiz: Understood. Let's talk about cache key normalization. How aggressive should we be at redacting variables?
[05:15] Priya Nair: Start conservative: redact emails, long identifiers, and ephemeral tokens. Normalize whitespace and punctuation. Then run a small A/B experiment: keying A - exact templates, keying B - normalized placeholders. Measure precision/recall of cache hits against model output differences. We have tooling to score output divergence.
[05:33] Maya Li: That scoring tooling — can you share it?
[05:35] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll attach the eval harness and sample Jupyter in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[05:39] Jordan Hayes: Quick question on metrics: what telemetry do we expose?
[05:42] Priya Nair: We surface token-level latency, prefix hit-rate, KV blob sizes, cache eviction events, per-tenant namespace metrics, and per-model quant-tag counts. Also trace IDs to link specific inference requests to cache hits/misses.
[05:55] Owen Brooks: Does the telemetry include raw prompts? We have privacy concerns.
[05:58] Priya Nair: By default no — traces contain hashes and non-PII metadata. You can opt-in to capture raw prompts for debugging in a controlled way, stored encrypted and with TTL.
[06:09] Daniel Ortiz: On networking — if we run in our VPC how is synchronization done between Private nodes?
[06:14] Priya Nair: For VPC/private we deploy a cache agent that talks to local disk and optionally to a replicated backing store. Synchronization uses secure channels, mTLS, and your VPC peering or direct connect. We can size replication windows to minimize cross-AZ traffic.
[06:28] Jordan Hayes: Let's run a concrete scenario: 300 rps with 75% of requests being continuations of open sessions; median prefix length 240. What hit-rate and latency can we realistically expect?
[06:39] Priya Nair: If caching is tuned and template reuse is high, ballpark 60%+ prefix hits. With on-node RAM cache and NVMe backing, p95 under 100ms is achievable for hit paths. Misses will pay model compute cost — for that we recommend burst capacity and model variants with smaller context for cheap heads.
[06:55] Maya Li: About model variants — if a miss falls back to a smaller model, how do you preserve quality?
[06:59] Priya Nair: We support routing policies: canary -> full model for a percentage, or fallback to a compatible distilled model only for non-critical routes. Also we track quality drift via evals; if you see regressions we'll pause fallback.
[07:13] Daniel Ortiz: Security question: if we run a shared Dedicated pool with multiple tenants, what certifications and logging can we get for compliance?
[07:20] Jordan Hayes: We provide SOC2 Type II, ISO 27001 summaries, and full audit logs per-tenant. We also support VPC isolation and private control plane for strict customers.
[07:29] Maya Li: For a pilot, we'd like to run a 2-week bounded test with our traffic, and you'd run your prefix-caching instrumentation and share results. Is that feasible?
[07:36] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Typical pilot steps: 1) sample prompt dataset and infra specs, 2) Redwood runs offline sim for hit-rate estimates, 3) small on-prem or dedicated pilot with monitoring, 4) iterate keying rules. We'll provide the simulation harness and a recommended config.
[07:51] Owen Brooks: For the on-prem run — we prefer zero data leave policy. Can you guarantee logs don't leave our VPC?
[07:57] Jordan Hayes: Yes — with Private deployments logs can stay in your VPC. We'll document the flow in the security packet.
[08:03] Maya Li: One more thing — do prefix caches create GDPR or data-retention implications? If we cache user content, that's personal data.
[08:11] Priya Nair: Good call. We recommend TTLs aligned with retention policies and encryption-at-rest. Also provide tools to purge keys for subject access requests. We'll include purge APIs in the doc.
[08:21] Daniel Ortiz: Anything else around ops we should know?
[08:24] Priya Nair: For ops, you'll want to tune eviction thresholds, compression ratios, and prefilling lists. We'll help with with recommended defaults which we've included in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[08:34] Jordan Hayes: Ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:37] Jordan Hayes: Action items: Priya will run the 1k-conversation sim; Maya, please send prompt templates and tenant identifiers; Owen confirm VPC/network specs; Jordan will send security docs and pricing. We aim to kick off pilot week of Nov 24 if specs are ready.
[08:52] Maya Li: Sounds good.
[08:54] Daniel Ortiz: Good session, thanks.
[08:56] Owen Brooks: Thanks.
[08:57] Priya Nair: I'll upload the benchmark spreadsheet and harness, link is in the notes.
[09:01] Jordan Hayes: Cool. We'll follow up with calendar invite for the pilot kickoff and a 2-hour on-prem benchmark slot. Thanks everyone.

End notes:
- Benchmarks and eval harness will be shared: https://redwood.share/prefix-cache-benchmarks-2025
- Security packet (SOC2/ISO, network diagrams, KMS integration) to be sent by Jordan: expected 2025-11-21
- Pilot tentative start: week of 2025-11-24

Recording quality notes: occasional transcription errors ("KV cash" instead of "KV cache", "quant tag" transcribed as "count tag" in one segment), speaker overlaps near the end.
